title: The Spatial Scaling of Species' Climatic Niche Geometry
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Climatic associations of species, particularly the geometry of their climatic niches (e.g., niche breadth and shape), are central ecological characteristics and key to robust assessment and forecasting of biodiversity. While climatic niches are known to depend on spatial grain, a consensus on the generality of this dependence and its underlying drivers remains elusive.

Location

Western Hemisphere.

Time Period

1981–2018.

Major Taxa Studied

Birds (Aves).

Methods

We developed a quantitative framework to measure and predict the spatial scaling of species' realized climatic niche geometry. We examined variation in niche breadth and shape across a two-order-of-magnitude grain size gradient (1–100 km) for 1810 bird species across the Western Hemisphere. We tested the hypotheses that the magnitude and slope of spatial scaling in niche geometry are primarily driven by three key factors: (1) geographic range size, (2) habitat specialization and (3) landscape environmental heterogeneity. We further evaluated whether readily available coarse-grain data can reliably predict fine-grain niche breadth using these spatial scaling relationships.

Results

We found that for a quarter of the studied species, realized niche breadths differed by at least twofold across the 1–100 km grain gradient. Species occupying environmentally heterogeneous landscapes, with restricted geographic ranges and specialized habitat requirements, showed greater sensitivity of niche geometry to spatial grain. Furthermore, when combined with species' ecological and geographical attributes, these spatial scaling relationships allow robust prediction of fine-grain niche breadth using coarse-grain data.

Main Conclusions

Our results show that the spatial scaling of climatic niche geometry differs substantially across species with divergent landscape and ecological attributes. Future niche-based studies should explicitly account for grain-dependence. When fine-grain occurrence data are unavailable, cross-grain data integration can effectively mitigate scale-driven biases in niche estimates.
